Apple Health

01 · About

About Apple Health

The Apple Health app serves as Apple's centralized digital health platform, designed to help users understand, track and manage their overall well-being by providing access to:

  • Health Data Dashboard
  • Activity & Fitness Tracking
  • Vitals & Health Metrics
  • Medical Records & Health Sharing

Scope of the study

What we cover

  • Feature discoverability
  • Dashboard organisation
  • Pain points in varying sections
  • Overall clutter of the UI
  • Content clarity

What we don't

  • Inner data organisation
  • Third party portals
  • Graphic redesign

02 · Secondary research

What the internet already knew

We analysed App Store reviews for a basic understanding of the problem, ran a heuristics analysis, and compared similar health apps for structure, features and user preferences. Five published case studies shaped our starting hypotheses.

Apple Health UX Case Study · Nan Cao

Users face cognitive overload due to dense, unfiltered health metrics
Data is fragmented across multiple layers, reducing accessibility
Navigation lacks a clear mental model, forcing users to explore blindly
Important metrics are not prioritised, making all data feel equally important

The app prioritizes data collection over data comprehension, creating friction in everyday use.

The interface assumes users already understand what to look for, rather than guiding them. This creates a high cognitive burden, especially for casual users.

Shift from a data repository model to a guided insight system with prioritised, structured information

Apple Health Interaction Concept · Chris Rusnak

Grouping metrics into macro categories improves navigability
Collapsible components reduce visual clutter without removing data
Use of motion and transitions helps communicate hierarchy
Emphasis on progressive disclosure (show less → reveal more)

Interaction design (not just layout) can significantly reduce complexity in data-heavy interfaces.

Users don't struggle with volume alone. They struggle with how information unfolds over time. Static layouts fail to guide attention.

Introduce dynamic hierarchy where interaction patterns actively shape user understanding

Apple Health Redesign Concept · Design Bootcamp

Interface feels visually cluttered despite minimal styling
Layout lacks clear structure and grouping logic
Users experience friction in basic navigation tasks
The app fails to deliver on its promise of being intuitive and user-friendly

There is a disconnect between Apple's design philosophy (simplicity) and the actual user experience.

Minimalism alone does not guarantee usability. Without clear hierarchy and intentional grouping, minimal UI can still feel chaotic.

Replace aesthetic minimalism with functional clarity and structured layouts

Apple Health UX Case Study · Kylie Beauchamp

Users lack spatial awareness (don't know where they are in the app)
Heavy dependence on search indicates poor navigation design
UI elements appear interactive but lack clear affordances
No clear entry point or dashboard logic

The interface breaks fundamental usability principles like clarity, feedback and affordance.

The app violates core UX heuristics (visibility, consistency, feedback), forcing users to rely on trial-and-error interaction.

Reinforce predictability and system feedback through clearer navigation states and interactive cues

Apple Health UX Case Study · Amanda Cudzinovic

Core features are buried within layers of secondary data
Lack of clear categorization system
Interface feels overloaded with non-essential information
Users struggle to identify primary vs secondary data

The app fails to balance depth of information with ease of use.

Not all data should be treated equally. By presenting everything at the same level, the app removes decision-making cues.

Introduce tiered information architecture (primary / secondary / advanced data layers)

03 · Primary research

Twelve people, one dashboard

12users

Sample size

4 · 18–25 yr olds 3 · 26–35 yr olds 5 · 36–45 yr olds

Sampling criteria

  • Age groups representing typical health-app users
  • Mix of beginners, intermediate and advanced health-focused users
  • Individuals with different goals (weight loss, fitness, condition tracking)
  • Users with varying tech familiarity

User segments

Fitness enthusiasts
Track workouts, steps, sleep, or heart rate
People with chronic conditions
Log symptoms, medication and health metrics
Working professionals
Follow guided workout plans
Seniors focused on wellness
Monitor nutrition, hydration & calorie intake
Health-conscious adopters
Access health tips & reminders
Patients tracking medication
Communicate progress with healthcare providers

Types of users

01

Occasional users

Less health-focused users who use Apple Health sporadically to check or track specific metrics, such as steps or sleep, when the need arises.

02

Regular users

Long-term users who rely on Apple Health daily as an integrated tool for monitoring, managing and acting on their overall health data.

A casual health tracker who uses Apple Health because it came with her devices, not by choice. She wants to build small wellness habits like walking more, sleeping better and keeping track of her cycle, but avoids anything that feels complicated. 04 · Card sorting

Five people sorted every card

Each participant grouped the app's features in a way that made sense to them. Their groupings told us where the current labels and categories break down.

Repeated categories and unclear terminology caused confusion and navigation issues.
Wanted frequently used metrics easily accessible at higher levels.
Expected Profile to be a separate space with no repetition.
Felt overwhelmed by too many micro-categories, preferring fewer groupings.
Preferred organisation by purpose or context rather than strict system-based grouping.
Suggested Browse as a content-focused section (Trends, Articles, etc.).
Some labels were misleading or ambiguous.
Desired a more structured and intuitive layout overall.
Needed a dedicated tab for adding and inputting data.

05 · Site map & IA

A home for every metric

The card-sort groupings became a new site map and a final information architecture: a dedicated tab for logging data, a separate Profile, a content-focused Browse, and frequently used metrics lifted to the top level. Community features give the app a social layer.

Ten moments, drawn out

Each scenario frames a real-world need from the interviews, a storyboard shows how it plays out, and a user flow compares today's path with the redesigned one.

07 · Design system & wireframes

From grey boxes to glowing cards

We followed Apple's iOS UI guidelines as the framework and built on top of it: SF Pro Display and SF Pro Rounded for type, the familiar health icon set, and a soft gradient card for every metric.
